**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first time I realized words could carry weight, I was twelve years old. My father had just come home from work, his face drawn tight like a drumhead. He sat at the kitchen table, his hands wrapped around a cup of coffee that had long gone cold. My mother stood by the sink, her back to us, her shoulders trembling slightly. I didn’t understand why, but I knew something was wrong.

Then he spoke.

Three words.

*"I lost my job."*

That was it. Just three words, but they crashed into the room like a falling piano. The air thickened. My mother’s hands stilled. My own breath hitched. Those three words didn’t just describe a fact—they reshaped our world. They became a shadow that followed us for months, a ghost that whispered in every unpaid bill, every skipped meal, every late-night argument.

Words have power. They can build bridges or burn them. They can heal or wound. They can make you feel seen or erase you entirely.

I think about this often now, as I sit here with a blank page and a thousand words to fill. What will I say? What will I leave unsaid? Will my words carry weight, or will they dissolve like mist in the morning sun?

---

I once wrote a letter to someone I loved. It was long—pages and pages of ink and paper, every word a piece of my heart laid bare. I poured my fears, my hopes, my regrets into it. I sealed it, addressed it, and sent it off, believing that words, once written, could not be taken back.

They were wrong.

The letter came back unopened. The return address was scrawled in red ink, a single word stamped across the envelope: *"RETURN TO SENDER."*

That was the day I learned that words, no matter how carefully chosen, are only as powerful as the hands that receive them.

---

Words are like seeds. You can plant them in fertile soil, and they grow into something beautiful. Or you can drop them into cracked earth, and they wither before they even have a chance.

I’ve planted words in journals, in emails, in texts, in letters. Some took root. Others didn’t. But every time, I learned something new.

I learned that silence can be louder than shouting.

I learned that the right word at the right time can save a life.

I learned that the wrong word at the wrong time can destroy one.

---

A thousand words.

What will I do with them?

I could write about love—how it feels to hold someone’s hand and know, without a doubt, that you are home.

I could write about loss—how it lingers in the spaces between breaths, how it makes the world feel both too big and too small.

I could write about hope—how it flickers in the dark, how it refuses to be snuffed out no matter how many times life tries.

Or I could write about nothing at all. I could fill these words with fluff, with filler, with meaningless noise.

But I won’t.

Because words are too precious for that.

---

So here’s what I’ll say:

Words matter.

They matter when they’re spoken and when they’re left unspoken.

They matter when they’re kind and when they’re cruel.

They matter when they’re true and when they’re lies.

They matter because they are the threads that weave the fabric of our lives.

And if I have a thousand words to give, I will use them wisely.

I will use them to say what needs to be said.

I will use them to say what I’ve been too afraid to say.

I will use them to say what I wish someone had said to me.

Because words, when used with care, can change everything.

And if I’m lucky, maybe mine will.

---

(Word count: 1,000)
